The nineteen-sixty-four New York World's Fair returned to Flushing Meadows in Queens, a quarter-century after the iconic nineteen-thirty-nine exposition had transformed the site. This later fair celebrated technological progress and global culture during the height of the Space Race when American achievement in space seemed to symbolise unlimited possibility. President Lyndon B. Johnson officially opened the fair, which was themed to celebrate human progress, technological innovation, and world peace. Over fifty-one million visitors came to explore the fair's many exhibits and attractions. The fair's iconic symbol was the Unisphere, a massive hollow globe a hundred forty feet in diameter, designed by engineer and visionary Buckminster Fuller. The Unisphere represented global unity and interconnectedness, concepts central to the fair's vision. It remains in Flushing Meadows Park to this day and has become an enduring symbol of the fair and the era. The exposition hosted Futurama, which was an evolution of the famous nineteen-thirty-nine exhibit, showcasing advanced automation, robotics, and urban planning ideals developed from a quarter-century of technological progress. It included performances and cultural exhibits from participating nations, emphasising international cooperation and cultural exchange even during Cold War tensions that divided the world. The fair displayed cutting-edge technology including early computers, advanced consumer goods, and space-age design reflecting nineteen-sixties optimism and confidence about modernity. It marked one of the last grand American world's fairs before the format declined in popularity and frequency in subsequent decades.
